grade.rationale: Under the redline, the counterparty can no longer assign or delegate without Client's prior written consent, which satisfies the core rule. Client also gets an affiliate/successor carve-out, assigning without consent to an affiliate or to a successor in a merger or sale of substantially all assets, which matches the green standard. Making the consent requirement mutual while carving out an exception for Client is consistent with green. The drafting is clear and enforceable: a single operative sentence and a standard 'provided, however' proviso. Nothing outside assignment is changed. Minor drafting gaps: 'affiliate' is not defined unless it is defined elsewhere in the agreement, and there is no clause voiding a non-compliant assignment. Neither affects whether the redline meets green.

redline.new_text: 9.8 Assignment. Neither Party may assign its rights or delegate any of its duties under this Agreement without the prior written consent of the other Party; provided, however, that Client may assign this Agreement without consent to an affiliate or to a successor in connection with a merger or sale of substantially all of its assets.
redline.explanation: The draft is one-sided: Client cannot assign without consent while CC-Pharming can assign freely. The edit makes the consent requirement mutual, so CC-Pharming needs iBio's prior written consent to assign, and adds a Client-only carve-out for affiliates and for successors by merger or sale of substantially all assets. The existing prohibition on delegating duties is kept for both Parties.
optional_suggestions: Consider adding a sentence that any permitted assignee must assume this Agreement's obligations in writing.
If CC-Pharming pushes back on the affiliate carve-out, accept notice to CC-Pharming after the assignment instead of deleting the carve-out, but do not give up the successor carve-out.
Do not accept a reciprocal carve-out for CC-Pharming unless it includes change-of-control or competitor protection for iBio.

history.judge_rationale: Section 9.8 requires prior written consent from the other Party before either Party may assign or delegate, so the Counterparty cannot assign without Client's consent. It also gives Client the right to assign without consent to an affiliate or to a successor in a merger or sale of substantially all its assets. This matches the ideal clause.
suggestions: Consider adding a sentence that any permitted assignee must assume this Agreement's obligations in writing.
If CC-Pharming pushes back on the affiliate carve-out, accept notice to CC-Pharming after the assignment instead of deleting the carve-out, but do not give up the successor carve-out.
Do not accept a reciprocal carve-out for CC-Pharming unless it includes change-of-control or competitor protection for iBio.

history.judge_rationale: Section 2(d) gives Erchonia (Client) or its independent auditor the right to inspect, copy and audit Distributor's books and records on 30 days' written notice, once per calendar year, during normal business hours. Distributor must keep the records for the term plus two years. This matches the ideal clause and has no heavy restrictions such as counterparty-approved auditors or cost shifting.
added_outside: Inspection right is limited to no more than once per calendar year and to normal business hours (restrictions on the audit right)
Requires thirty (30) days' prior written notice, which is longer and more formal than 'reasonable notice' as the rule requires
Distributor must maintain books and records for the term plus two (2) years (new record retention obligation, beneficial but beyond the rule)
Right extends to an independent auditor and includes copying (beyond the rule, though favorable to Client)
suggestions: Add a cost-shift: Distributor reimburses reasonable audit costs and promptly pays any shortfall if an audit shows an underpayment above 5%.
Add that the auditor is not subject to Distributor's approval, with a customary confidentiality undertaking as the only condition.
Extend the audit right to cover Distributor's sales and customer records under Section 1(d) expressly, and make Distributor's sales reports auditable.

Clarify that Distributor's records must be made available at Distributor's address or electronically, and that 'Counterparty' should be conformed to the defined term 'Distributor' in the first sentence of c6.

history.judge_rationale: Client (Erchonia) has a right to inspect and audit the Distributor's (counterparty's) books and records relating to the Agreement on reasonable notice. The clause is not heavily restricted: there is no counterparty-approved auditor requirement, no long notice period and no cost-shifting. It also gives the counterparty a reciprocal inspection right over Erchonia's performance information, which is not a material concern. It uses the undefined term 'Counterparty' for the Distributor, but the meaning is clear in context.
added_outside: The audit right extends to 'inspect and audit' the Counterparty's 'books and records', which is arguably broader than the rule's 'relevant records'. It is still limited to records relating to this Agreement and to reasonable notice, so the scope is only marginally broader.
Paragraph breaks and spacing between items e, f and g were collapsed into a single paragraph. This is formatting only, with no substantive effect.
suggestions: Add the playbook's preferred terms as a follow-on: thirty (30) days' prior written notice, once per calendar year, normal business hours, and a right to copy, as separate edits if the counterparty accepts the core right.
Add a right for an independent auditor, subject only to a customary confidentiality undertaking, and reject any counterparty approval of the auditor in its sole discretion.
Require the Distributor to keep books and records for the Term plus about two (2) years, and tie the audit right to the records described in Section 1(d).

Add a cost-shift: Erchonia bears audit costs unless the audit shows an underpayment above 5%, in which case the Distributor reimburses reasonable audit costs and promptly pays the shortfall with interest.
Correct the undefined term 'Counterparty' to 'Distributor' in the existing sentence, and address the duplicated 'upon reasonable notice' wording, in a conforming cleanup.

history.judge_rationale: Client (Erchonia) may inspect, copy and audit the counterparty's (Distributor's) books and records on reasonable notice, once per calendar year during normal business hours. This matches the golden rule's substance. The clause uses the undefined term 'Counterparty' and has no restrictions such as counterparty-approved auditors or cost-shifting, so it is not heavily restricted. Distributor's record-keeping obligations in c5 support the right.
added_outside: Audit right limited to no more than once per calendar year
Audit right limited to normal business hours
Right extends to copying records (inspect, copy and audit), which is beyond a simple audit right but arguably within it
Scope limited to the Counterparty's books and records relating to this Agreement (narrower than 'any records')
Formatting changes: paragraph breaks removed and clauses e, f, g merged into one paragraph (non-substantive)
suggestions: Add a record-retention obligation requiring the Counterparty to keep relevant records for the Term plus about two years.

Add a cost-shift so Erchonia bears audit costs only if the audit shows no material discrepancy (underpayment under 5%), with the Counterparty reimbursing costs and paying any shortfall with interest if the threshold is exceeded.

Accept a Counterparty right to object to a named auditor only for a genuine conflict of interest, or require a customary confidentiality undertaking from the auditor, and resist any approval right in the Counterparty's sole discretion.
Consider making the notice period an express thirty (30) days rather than 'reasonable notice' to match the playbook preferred position.

history.judge_rationale: Section 14 sets a mutual cap at 12 months' Fees, with carve-outs for breach of confidentiality, indemnification obligations, and gross negligence or willful misconduct. This matches the golden rule. The cap is measured by 'Fees', but the agreement is a strategic alliance with a right of first offer, so it is unclear whether any Fees are paid or payable, which may make the cap illusory. The other excerpts also reference Sections 9 and 11, which are not shown. Even so, the clause's legal effect matches the rule.
suggestions: Confirm the waiver of claims for property damage and its gross negligence/willful misconduct exception that the playbook references appear elsewhere in the agreement, and preserve them unchanged.
Consider adding a fixed dollar floor alongside the 12-month fee measure (greater-of formulation) as a fallback position, without lowering the 12-month lookback.
Consider a separate, higher super-cap for data or confidentiality breaches as a fallback, provided the indemnity and gross negligence/willful misconduct carve-outs remain.
Consider replacing the term 'Fees' with a defined term check so that 'Fees paid or payable' is clearly defined elsewhere in the agreement.
Consider correcting the stray '7' following the Section 14 acknowledgment in the final paragraph of the section.

history.judge_rationale: Section 14 sets a mutual aggregate liability cap equal to fees paid or payable in the preceding 12 months. It carves out confidentiality breaches, indemnification obligations, and gross negligence or willful misconduct, and the carve-outs apply equally to both parties. This matches the golden rule. One caveat is that the agreement appears to provide for few or no 'Fees', which could make the cap nominal in practice, but the clause itself is a standard mutual cap.
added_outside: Statement that neither Party's liability for matters in (a)-(c) is subject to the cap, making Client's liability for confidentiality breach, indemnification and gross negligence/willful misconduct uncapped (the rule requires carve-outs but does not require that Client's exposure be unlimited in a way that strips the existing protection; this is consistent with standard mutual carve-outs but is a substantive change in Client's exposure)
suggestions: Consider adding a fixed dollar floor alongside the 12-month fee measure, using the greater of the two, to strengthen the cap.
Consider a separate, higher super-cap for data or confidentiality breaches as a fallback if Hyatt resists uncapped confidentiality exposure.
Consider confirming that the Section 14 waiver and its gross negligence/willful misconduct exception are preserved in any later amendment.

history.judge_rationale: Section 14 sets a mutual cap at 12 months' fees, with carve-outs for confidentiality, indemnification, and gross negligence/willful misconduct that apply equally to both parties, matching the rule. However, the proviso is internally contradictory: it says liability for the carved-out matters 'shall remain subject to the cap', which negates the carve-outs. Also, the Agreement appears to have no 'Fees' (it is a right of first offer arrangement), so the cap's base is unclear and could be zero. The section is titled 'Waiver of Non-compensatory Damages' but the waiver text is not shown. These ambiguities need a lawyer's attention.
outside_changes: Client's liability for any matter in (a)-(c) remains subject to the cap (Client's liability is capped even for carve-out matters)
added_outside: Revised proviso states that any liability of either Party for matters in (a)-(c) 'shall remain subject to the cap', which contradicts the carve-out sentence, creates an internal conflict, and extends the cap to both Parties' carve-out liability (arguably nullifying the carve-outs, including those against Hyatt)
suggestions: Consider proposing that the carve-outs in (a) through (c) sit wholly outside the cap for both Parties, which is the playbook's preferred formulation, and negotiate for it as a separate point since it would expose Client's own confidentiality, indemnity and gross negligence liability without limit.
Consider proposing a separate, higher super-cap for data or confidentiality breaches as a fallback if the counterparty pushes back on the uncapped carve-outs.
Consider confirming that the stray reference '7' at the end of Section 14 in the following paragraph is a formatting artifact and should be removed in the final execution version.

history.judge_rationale: Segment c54n gives Client a termination right on a counterparty change of control. It covers mergers, acquisitions, and transfers of more than 50% of voting securities, applies regardless of acquirer identity (competitors included), and requires prompt notice from the counterparty. This matches the golden rule. Segment c54 also lets the other Party terminate if Client undergoes a change of control, but that is a separate, reciprocal provision and does not remove Client's right.
added_outside: Requirement that the other Party give Client prompt written notice of any change of control (a notice obligation, arguably ancillary to the termination right but not itself required by the rule, though it favors Client).
90-day exercise window running from Client's receipt of notice (a time limit on Client's termination right, which narrows the right beyond what the rule requires).

Definition of change of control as any merger, acquisition, or transfer of more than 50% of voting securities (a definitional choice; the rule does not specify it, and it could be narrower than other forms of change of control such as asset sales or de facto control).
suggestions: Consider deleting the counterparty's termination right and Client's consent restriction on change of control in Section 9.3, since they run against Client; this was not done here to keep the change minimal.
Correct the party-name inconsistency in Section 9.3, which refers to Client although the parties are PURCHASER and Sony Electronics Inc.; align the defined terms throughout the agreement.
Fix the garbled text in Section 9.3 ('on condition that it provides the 14') and the stray section numbering that follows it.
Define 'change of control' in Section 1 so the term is used consistently and the competitor concept is defined, for example by reference to a named competitor list amendable only by mutual agreement.
Consider adding a Client termination right on counterparty change of control with a longer exercise window or a consent right if the acquirer is a competitor, as a fallback position.

history.judge_rationale: Section 9.3 contains a sentence giving Client an unconditional right to terminate on written notice if the counterparty undergoes a change of control, regardless of who the acquirer is. That matches the golden rule. The same section also gives the counterparty a termination right if Client undergoes a change of control. That is a reciprocal burden on Client, but it does not weaken Client's own right.
added_outside: The phrase "Notwithstanding the foregoing" overrides any prior provisions in the agreement without specifying which ones, which may reach beyond the rule's scope (e.g., could override notice, cure, or exclusivity terms).
The phrase "regardless of the identity of the acquirer" is an added qualifier; it is arguably consistent with the rule but is not strictly required.
The clause references "IP Agreement" and "other Party" as terms that may not be defined in the surrounding contract.
suggestions: Consider adding a 90-day window after Client receives written notice of the change of control to exercise the termination right, consistent with the playbook, though this was left out to keep the change minimal.
Consider adding a requirement that the other Party give Client prompt written notice of any change of control, so Client knows when the right arises.

Consider defining change of control (for example, a merger, acquisition, or transfer of more than 50% of voting securities, or a sale of substantially all assets) so the trigger is not left open to dispute.

Consider deleting or narrowing the reciprocal provision in Section 9.3 that lets the other Party terminate on a change of control of Client, and the consent requirement on Client's assignment, since these run against Client.
Consider correcting the drafting inconsistency in Section 9.3, which refers to Client although the parties are PURCHASER and SONY Electronics Inc.
Consider adding a consent or termination right for Client where the acquirer is a competitor of Client, with a Named Competitor list that only Client or both parties may amend.

history.judge_rationale: Segment c54n gives Client a termination right if the counterparty undergoes a change of control. The term is defined as any merger, acquisition or transfer of more than 50% of voting securities. The right applies regardless of who the acquirer is, including a competitor, and the counterparty must give prompt notice. This matches the golden rule. Segment c54 separately lets the counterparty terminate if Client undergoes a change of control, but that does not remove Client's own right.
added_outside: Obligation on the counterparty to give Client prompt written notice of any change of control (a notice covenant not strictly required by the rule, though it supports it and benefits Client)
90-day exercise window after Client receives notice, which limits Client's termination right (a time limit not required by the rule)

Definition of change of control as any merger, acquisition, or transfer of more than 50% of voting securities (a definitional choice; the rule does not specify a definition, and it is broad because it includes any merger or acquisition regardless of size)
suggestions: Correct the drafting inconsistency in Section 9.3 by replacing 'Client' with the correct Party name (PURCHASER or SONY) so the existing change-of-control language is not read against the wrong party.
Consider deleting the Section 9.3 counterparty termination right triggered by a change of control of Client, and the related restriction on Client's assignment, since these run against Client.
Consider adding a defined term for 'change of control' and confirming that 'IP Agreement' and 'Party' are defined consistently with the Asset Purchase Agreement.
Consider having the Section 9.1 notice mechanics expressly apply to the change-of-control notices required by the new clause.

history.judge_rationale: The agreement requires each Participant to maintain commercial general liability insurance at its own expense, with minimum limits of $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 aggregate. The Joint Venture is named as additional insured, and certificates are delivered on request. This matches the ideal clause. The additional insured is the Joint Venture rather than Client individually, but Client is the Joint Venture, so the effect is the same.
added_outside: Insurance must be maintained at Participant's own expense
Coverage must be maintained at all times during the term of the Agreement
Carrier must be of good standing
suggestions: Add statutory workers' compensation coverage where applicable, per the playbook's preferred position.
Add an express obligation to deliver certificates of insurance before activities begin, and notice to Client of cancellation or material reduction, in c34.
State expressly in c34 that the insurance does not limit the Participant's liability or indemnities.
Confirm that the Participant named as additional insured is the counterparty to the JVP obligations, since c34 refers to 'each Participant' and the Joint Venture as the insured.
Correct the mislabeled 'Name' and 'Liability Insurance' headings and the stray numbering in c33 and c34 in a clean-up pass, without changing substance.

history.judge_rationale: Clause c34 requires each Participant to maintain Required Coverage throughout the term. c2 defines Required Coverage as commercial general liability insurance of at least $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 in the annual aggregate. The Joint Venture must be named as an additional insured, and certificates are to be delivered on request. This matches the ideal clause. The additional insured is the Joint Venture rather than Client individually, but Client is the Joint Venture, so the effect is the same.
added_outside: Restriction of Required Coverage to commercial general liability insurance only, which eliminates the broader 'kinds' of coverage previously contemplated (e.g., property, professional, workers' compensation) rather than just adding minimums
No additional insured requirement for Client/Joint Venture was added (rule says ideally), so this is an omission rather than an addition
suggestions: Add that the Participant maintains the coverage at its own expense, to make the cost allocation explicit.
Add a carrier good-standing or minimum AM Best rating requirement so the insurer is not left to the Participant's discretion.
Add that certificates of insurance are provided before the Participant begins activities, not only on request.
Add notice to the Joint Venture of cancellation or material reduction of the coverage.
Add that the insurance does not limit the Participant's liability or indemnities under the Agreement.
Add statutory workers' compensation coverage where applicable.
Clarify whether the obligation is owed by the Participant generally or by a specific counterparty, since the JVP parties are described collectively.
Consider whether the Required Coverage definition should specify the kinds of coverage, not only the general liability line.
Consider replacing the phrase 'Required Coverage' in c34 with the defined term only if the drafting team wants to tie the additional-insured duty explicitly to the new limits.

history.judge_rationale: Each Participant must maintain Required Coverage, defined as at least $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 in the annual aggregate. The Joint Venture must be named as an additional insured, and certificates of insurance are delivered on request. This matches the ideal clause. The type of insurance is not specified, but the limits are stated.
added_outside: The revision does not name Client/Joint Venture as additional insured. This is not an addition but a missed opportunity under the rule's ideal; nothing outside the rule has been added.
suggestions: Add in c34 that the insurance is maintained at the Participant's own expense and that certificates are delivered before activities begin, not only on request.
Add a notice requirement in c34 for cancellation or material reduction of Required Coverage.
Add that Required Coverage does not limit the Participant's liability or indemnities under this Agreement.
Consider specifying a carrier of good standing and, where applicable, statutory workers' compensation coverage.

Consider clarifying in c34 that the additional-insured status for the Joint Venture is to be maintained for the full term, and that the Joint Venture is not required to bear any premium or deductible.

grade.rationale: In this agreement, Client is the Distributor, which receives Products from the Company. The Company is therefore the counterparty. The redline obliges the Company to carry CGL insurance at its own expense for the full term. It sets specified minimum limits of $1M per occurrence and $2M in the aggregate, and it names the Distributor as additional insured, so it meets the green standard. The drafting is clear, enforceable, and consistent with the agreement's defined terms. It places it as new section 9.05 without disturbing other provisions. It does not go beyond the rule: it adds no indemnity, certificate, or other unrelated obligations. One minor gap is that it does not cover products liability or require certificates or notice of cancellation, but that does not defeat green.

redline.new_text: 9.05. Insurance. The Company will, at its own expense and throughout the term of this Agreement, maintain commercial general liability insurance with limits of not less than $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 in the annual aggregate, naming the Distributor as an additional insured.
redline.explanation: The agreement has no insurance maintenance obligation on the Company. The rule requires a stated insurance obligation with fixed minimum limits, ideally naming Client (Distributor) as additional insured. The single new Section 9.05 fits the existing numbering gap between 9.04 and 9.07, places the obligation on the Company, and sets the market-ask limits. The prior redline's extra terms (workers' compensation, certificates, cancellation notice, carrier rating, and non-limitation language) are removed as beyond the rule, so they are not in this redline.
optional_suggestions: Consider adding a requirement for statutory workers' compensation insurance where applicable, as a separate negotiated item.
Consider requiring certificates of insurance before any Products are shipped and upon request, with written notice to the Distributor of cancellation or material reduction of coverage.
Consider requiring the insurer to be of good standing and stating that the insurance does not limit the Company's liability or indemnities under Sections 4.01 and 4.02.
Consider a fallback to additional-insured status 'where commercially available' if the Company resists naming the Distributor.

history.judge_rationale: Section 9.05 requires the Company (the counterparty) to carry commercial general liability insurance with stated minimum limits ($1M per occurrence / $2M aggregate). It must name the Distributor (Client) as an additional insured, provide certificates before shipment and on request, and give notice of cancellation or reduction. This matches the ideal clause and the green rubric.
added_outside: Statutory workers' compensation insurance requirement
Obligation to provide certificates of insurance before any Products are shipped and upon request
Obligation to give written notice of cancellation or material reduction of coverage
Carrier of good standing requirement
Clause stating that insurance does not limit the Company's liability or indemnities
suggestions: Consider adding a Company covenant to name the Distributor as additional insured on a blanket endorsement basis if the Company's carrier will not otherwise issue a named endorsement.
Consider requiring the Company to provide the Distributor with copies of the actual policy endorsements, not just certificates.
Consider aligning Section 4.01 and 9.03 indemnities with the new insurance clause so the Company's indemnity obligations are expressly backed by the coverage required in Section 9.05.
Consider adding a Company obligation to maintain product liability coverage for the Snotarator Products, given the medical-device nature of the Products.
Consider whether the Section 3.02 transit insurance allocation to the Distributor should be limited to cargo in transit after delivery to the carrier, to avoid overlap with the new Company coverage.

history.judge_rationale: Section 9.05 requires the Company (the counterparty supplying goods) to maintain CGL insurance throughout the term with stated minimum limits ($1M per occurrence / $2M aggregate) and to name the Distributor (Client) as an additional insured. This matches the ideal clause. The only gap is that there is no express obligation to provide certificates of insurance on request, which is a minor omission.
suggestions: Consider adding a requirement for statutory workers' compensation insurance where applicable, as a separate negotiated item.
Consider requiring certificates of insurance before any Products are shipped and upon request, with written notice to the Distributor of cancellation or material reduction of coverage.
Consider requiring the insurer to be of good standing and stating that the insurance does not limit the Company's liability or indemnities under Sections 4.01 and 4.02.
Consider a fallback to additional-insured status 'where commercially available' if the Company resists naming the Distributor.

history.judge_rationale: The form of Assignment (Exhibit C) contains a present assignment of Deliverables and Work Product to the Assignee (Client), with Pre-Existing Materials excluded but licensed back on a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free basis. That matches the rule's effect. The text appears to be a template mismatched to a marketing and contract-assignment deal, since the main agreement has no deliverables ownership clause. The exhibit's usage is somewhat odd, but it is a present assignment with a licence back for the carve-out.
outside_changes: No licence, express or implied, to Pre-Existing Materials is granted to Assignee under this Agreement
added_outside: Express grant of a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to Assignee to use Pre-Existing Materials solely to the extent embedded in or necessary to use the Assigned Work Product
suggestions: Define 'Deliverables' and 'Work Product' in the Assignment, or by reference to the Marketing Agreement, so the scope of the assignment is certain.
Correct the cross-reference in paragraph 1(b) ('the Assigned Rights') to the defined term 'Assigned Work Product'.

Consider making the Pre-Existing Materials licence non-exclusive, transferable and sublicensable to Affiliates and successors, so Client can use and maintain the deliverables after an assignment or change of control.
Add a short further-assurances covenant requiring the Assignor to execute documents needed to perfect the assignment of the Assigned Work Product.

Confirm in the main Marketing Agreement that the Assigned Work Product under this form is covered by the Party-level IP ownership terms, since the main agreement has no general work product ownership clause.

history.judge_rationale: The form of Assignment (Exhibit C) contains a present assignment of Deliverables and Work Product to the Assignee (Client). However, it excludes the Assignor's Pre-Existing Materials (frameworks, libraries, tools, methodologies, know-how) and expressly grants no licence, express or implied, to them. This is a significant carve-out without a licence back, which falls squarely within the yellow rubric. The assignment also sits in an exhibit form that appears oddly drafted, and the main Marketing Agreement has no IP ownership clause for deliverables.
suggestions: Add an express perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to Assignee to use Pre-Existing Materials solely to the extent embedded in or necessary to use the Assigned Work Product, as a fallback-level protection; this should be negotiated as a separate change to the no-licence sentence.
Define 'Deliverables' and 'Work Product' in the Assignment so the scope of the present assignment is certain.
Add a short further-assurances covenant requiring the Assignor to execute documents reasonably required to perfect the assignment of the Assigned Work Product.
Confirm the Main Marketing Agreement contains a matching ownership allocation for work product, since it currently has no general IP ownership clause.

history.judge_rationale: The form of Assignment (Exhibit C) contains a present assignment of Deliverables and Work Product to the Assignee (Client), with pre-existing materials excluded but licensed back on a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free basis. However, this appears in an exhibit template that seems mismatched to the Marketing Agreement, which has no deliverables or work-product concept. The body of the Marketing Agreement has no IP ownership clause, and the Assignment's provision is tied to a different subject matter. The language is ambiguous and may not operate as intended, so a lawyer should review it, even though the carve-out is properly licensed back.
outside_changes: No licence, express or implied, to Pre-Existing Materials is granted to Assignee under the Agreement
added_outside: Express grant to Assignee of a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use Pre-Existing Materials as embedded in or necessary to use the Deliverables and Assigned Work Product (not required by the rule, which concerns present assignment of deliverables/work product IP; the original already had a present assignment)
suggestions: Define 'Deliverables', 'Work Product' and 'Pre-Existing Materials' in the Assignment so the terms are not undefined.
Add a further-assurances covenant requiring the Assignor to execute documents needed to perfect the assignment.
Ask that the form's ownership allocation be carried into the main Marketing Agreement, which currently has no IP ownership clause for work product.
Conform the 'Assigned Rights' reference in the acceptance sentence of Section 1(a) to the defined term 'Assigned Work Product'.
Confirm that the licence survives termination and extends to sublicensing to Affiliates and SPVs.
